summary: Typed Wildcard FEC lets LDP request, withdraw or release all label bindings of a given FEC type. This RFC defines typed wildcard elements for the PWid and Generalized PWid FEC types used by pseudowires.

eli5.summary: Rather than withdrawing each tag one at a time, you can say take back all tags of this kind. This extends it to pseudowire tags.

questions: what is ldp typed wildcard fec
how to withdraw all pseudowire labels in ldp
what is the pwid fec element
subtitle: A compact LDP element that lets one message cover all pseudowire label bindings of a given type.

tldr.problem: LDP can use typed wildcards to act on all label bindings of one FEC element type, but each type needs its own definition, and the pseudowire FEC types (PWid and Generalized PWid) had none.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a Typed Wildcard FEC Element for PWid (0x80) and Generalized PWid (0x81). It carries a 15-bit PW type that scopes the wildcard, with 0x7FFF meaning all PW types.
tldr.outcome: One message can now check, withdraw or report status for many pseudowires at once, instead of one message per pseudowire.

today: RFC 6667 is a Proposed Standard published in July 2012. It has not been obsoleted or updated according to its metadata.

sections.title: The Gap in Typed Wildcards
sections.content:
An extension to the Label Distribution Protocol (LDP) in RFC 5918 defines a Typed Wildcard Forwarding Equivalence Class (FEC) Element. It is used to request, release or withdraw all label bindings for a given type of FEC element. A typed wildcard must be defined separately for each FEC element type.

RFC 4447 defines the PWid FEC Element and the Generalized PWid FEC Element but does not give them a typed wildcard format. This document supplies it. The procedures for processing are the same as RFC 5918 describes for any typed wildcard FEC element type.
sections.eli5: There was already a way to say take back all tags of one kind. But pseudowire tags had no way to say it, so this paper adds one.

sections.title: The Typed Wildcard PW FEC Element
sections.content:
The element has these fields: the Typed Wildcard type (one octet, 0x05), the PW FEC element type (one octet, 0x80 for PWid or 0x81 for Generalized PWid), a Len field (one octet, set to two), a reserved R bit and a 15-bit PW type.

Len is two because there is additional FEC information to scope the wildcard. The R bit MUST be zero on transmit and ignored on receipt. The PW type limits the operation to PWs of that type. It MUST be set to the Wildcard type 0x7FFF when all PW types are meant.

RFC 4447 also defines a PW Grouping ID TLV for wildcard withdrawal and status messages. When the typed wildcard for Generalized PWid is in use, that TLV MUST NOT be in the same message. A receiving LSR that sees it MUST ignore it silently and process the rest of the message.
sections.eli5: It is a short note with a few boxes: what kind of note it is, which kind of tag, and which sort of tunnel. One special value means every sort.

sections.title: Applicability
sections.content:
Earlier, RFC 4447 let a sender group pseudowires with a 32-bit Group ID in the PWid FEC Element, or with a PW Grouping ID TLV for the Generalized PWid FEC Element. This allows wildcard withdrawals and status messages for a group, for example after a physical port failure.

The typed wildcard gives similar function for label withdrawal and status notification, and it is more general. It also allows Typed Wildcard Label Request messages, and it allows Label TLVs to narrow the wildcard to FECs of that type that are bound to a given label.

The element may be used in any LDP message that has a FEC TLV as a mandatory or optional parameter. That includes label messages, notification messages carrying PW Status, and Address Withdraw messages used for VPLS MAC address withdrawal. In an Address Withdraw message, the MAC List TLV MUST contain an empty list.
sections.eli5: Before, you could only group tags by a number you chose in advance. Now you can also say all tags of this type, in many kinds of messages.

sections.title: Use Cases
sections.content:
The RFC gives four examples with two LSRs, A and B, sharing an LDP session for L2VPN pseudowire bindings.

  • Consistency check: A marks all Generalized PWid bindings learned from B as stale, then sends a Label Request with the typed wildcard and PW type 0x7FFF. B replays its bindings in Label Mapping messages, then sends an End-of-LIB notification. Any binding still stale at A is removed.
  • Graceful shutdown: A sends a Label Withdraw with typed wildcards for PWid and Generalized PWid. B deletes all of those bindings learned from A and answers with Label Release messages, with no session flap.
  • Wildcard PW status: after a global failure, one PW Status notification with the typed wildcard replaces one notification per PW, which eases scaling.
  • VPLS MAC withdrawal: one Address Withdraw can withdraw MAC addresses for all VPLS instances, or for all instances of a given PW type.
sections.eli5: Instead of knocking on every door, you can announce to the whole street at once: check your tags, drop all your tags, or this wire is broken.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content: The RFC says there are no new security considerations beyond those of the specifications it builds on: RFC 5036, RFC 4447, RFC 4762, RFC 5918 and RFC 5920. They apply to the PW typed wildcard FEC element types as well.
sections.eli5: This adds no new danger. The same safety rules as before still cover it.

viz.caption: TYPED WILDCARD FEC ELEMENT FOR PW FEC TYPES (RFC 6667)

fields.name: Type
fields.desc: PW FEC element type: 0x80 for PWid or 0x81 for Generalized PWid.

fields.name: Len
fields.desc: Additional FEC information to scope the wildcard.

fields.name: R
fields.desc: Reserved; MUST be zero on transmit and ignored on receipt.

fields.name: PW Type
fields.desc: Scopes the wildcard to one PW type; 0x7FFF means all types.
